patient.chief_complaint: Witnessed brief shaking then prolonged confusion and abnormal movements for 50 minutes, fever present
patient.history_present_illness: A 66-year-old Hispanic male retired mechanic was brought to the emergency department by his son, who witnessed a brief tonic-clonic seizure at home lasting approximately 2 minutes. The patient has no known history of epilepsy. His son reports that over the past 2 weeks, his father had been having progressive memory difficulty, confusion, and behavioral changes — he kept repeating questions, got lost driving to a familiar gas station, and had been sleeping 14-16 hours per day. He had also complained of intermittent headaches. No fever at home was noted initially. After the brief shaking stopped, the patient did not return to baseline. Instead, over the following 20 minutes, the son noticed his father making repetitive unusual hand and finger movements — rubbing his thumb and index finger together continuously — and intermittently smacking his lips. EMS temperature was 38.2°C. He has a history of type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia but no neurological conditions. He takes metformin and lisinopril. Recently, his primary care physician started him on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) for a urinary tract infection 12 days ago. He also takes over-the-counter cetirizine for seasonal allergies. No known immunosuppression. Son denies alcohol use, illicit drugs, or recent travel outside the state. No sick contacts. No known tuberculosis exposure. Family history: father had Alzheimer's dementia at 78. Wife died of breast cancer. Son and daughter healthy.

interactions: Acyclovir + TMP-SMX: Both are renally cleared via tubular secretion; concurrent use increases nephrotoxicity risk — competitive inhibition of tubular secretion reduces clearance of both agents
TMP-SMX + creatinine: TMP-SMX inhibits tubular creatinine secretion, causing falsely elevated serum creatinine — true GFR may be higher than creatinine-based estimates
Acyclovir + metformin: High-dose IV acyclovir-related nephrotoxicity risk necessitates holding metformin to prevent lactic acidosis
warnings: Concurrent use of acyclovir and TMP-SMX increases nephrotoxicity risk due to combined tubular secretion competition; close renal function monitoring is warranted.
Metformin should be withheld during high-dose IV acyclovir to reduce risk of lactic acidosis if renal impairment develops.
Monitor creatinine and BUN during IV acyclovir therapy; adequate hydration is recommended to reduce nephrotoxicity risk.

output.query: HSV encephalitis treatment acyclovir duration outcome NCSE

results.title: Herpes simplex encephalitis: diagnosis and treatment update
results.key_finding: IV acyclovir 10 mg/kg q8h for 14-21 days is the established treatment duration for herpes simplex encephalitis. Neurological sequelae including memory impairment and post-encephalitic epilepsy are reported in 30-40% of patients despite antiviral therapy. Non-convulsive seizure activity has been reported in HSV encephalitis and EEG monitoring is used for detection. Adjunctive corticosteroids remain of unproven benefit and are not standard of care.

output.summary: Herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1 predominantly in adults) is treated with IV acyclovir for 14-21 days; CSF HSV PCR is the diagnostic standard with sensitivity of 96-98% when performed within 2-10 days of symptom onset. Non-convulsive seizures and status epilepticus have been reported in the acute phase; antiseizure medications are used concurrently with antivirals for seizure management. Crystallization nephropathy is a recognized complication of IV acyclovir; adequate hydration reduces this risk. Post-encephalitic epilepsy and memory impairment are reported as sequelae in a significant proportion of survivors.

critical_actions: Empiric acyclovir IMMEDIATELY — fatal delay if HSV diagnosis missed
LP with HSV PCR — definitive diagnostic test
MRI brain with FLAIR + DWI — classic right temporal HSV-1 pattern
Stop TMP-SMX — nephrotoxicity with IV acyclovir; hold metformin
21-day acyclovir course — do NOT stop early when patient improves
contraindicated_actions: Delaying acyclovir pending MRI or LP results — HSV encephalitis is fatal without early treatment
Stopping acyclovir prematurely (before 21 days) — relapses are common; must complete full course
Continuing TMP-SMX with IV acyclovir — combined nephrotoxicity; also TMP elevates creatinine artifactually
key_reasoning_points: HSV-1 encephalitis classically affects temporal and frontal limbic structures — right or bilateral temporal FLAIR changes + behavioral symptoms + fever
NCSE complicating HSV encephalitis arises from acute temporal lobe destruction — treat both the infection (acyclovir) and the seizures (AED)
Empiric acyclovir should never wait for CSF results — mortality increases dramatically with every hour of delay
TMP-SMX falsely elevates creatinine and competes with acyclovir for tubular secretion — stop TMP-SMX during acyclovir therapy
Resident-level challenge: distinguish HSV encephalitis from autoimmune limbic encephalitis; both show temporal FLAIR changes; CSF HSV PCR is definitive

red_herrings.data_point: Procalcitonin 0.6 ng/mL (elevated) with WBC 11.8 and temperature 38.4°C
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests bacterial meningitis or sepsis, prompting empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics as primary treatment and potentially delaying acyclovir
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Procalcitonin mildly elevated but well below thresholds for bacterial meningitis (typically >2 ng/mL); WBC and temperature elevations are consistent with viral encephalitis; CSF lymphocytic pleocytosis and negative gram stain/culture confirm viral not bacterial etiology

red_herrings.data_point: Family history of Alzheimer's dementia + 2-week subacute cognitive decline (memory difficulty, confusion, behavioral changes, hypersomnia)
red_herrings.intended_effect: Suggests rapidly progressive Alzheimer's or prion disease (e.g., CJD), prompting dementia workup and cognitive referral rather than urgent encephalitis treatment
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: 2-week subacute timeline is too rapid for Alzheimer's (which progresses over months to years); fever, CSF pleocytosis, and positive HSV PCR confirm acute infectious encephalitis; family history of Alzheimer's is incidental
